data-sources-s1.title: Field notes from a market street (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
data-sources-s1.html: Saturday, 10 a.m., Market Street, the capital of Country A. I counted 42 stalls between the bus stop and the river. Most sell fruit, phone covers or clothes. Two stall owners told me they moved here last year because the old market was torn down for a parking garage. The street smells of grilled corn, and it is loud with music and bargaining. Shoppers say they come because "everything is cheaper than in the mall."

data-in-decisions-s2.title: Planning flood shelters with satellite images (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
data-in-decisions-s2.html: After heavy rains in an invented river town, the district office compared satellite images taken before and after the flood. The images showed which streets were under water and for how many days. Using a GIS, staff layered the flooded streets over the census count of people on each block. They chose three schools on high ground as shelters, each within a short walk of the blocks with the most people. One officer noted that clouds hid part of the town on the second day, so some flooding there may not have been recorded.

spatial-concepts-s1.title: Singapore: where the city sits (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
spatial-concepts-s1.html: Singapore is a small, mostly flat island at the southern tip of the Malay Peninsula, about 140 km north of the equator. Its south shore has deep water sheltered from storms, a good natural harbor. The island lies beside the Strait of Malacca, the narrow sea lane that ships use to travel between the Indian Ocean and the South China Sea. Ships carrying goods between Europe, the Middle East and East Asia pass close by, and many stop to load, unload and refuel.

human-environment-s2.title: The shrinking Aral Sea (written for practice, LevlPrep 2026)
human-environment-s2.html: The Aral Sea, on the border of Kazakhstan and Uzbekistan, was once one of the largest lakes in the world. From the 1960s, Soviet planners diverted the two rivers that fed it, the Amu Darya and the Syr Darya, to water huge new cotton fields. Cotton output rose. The sea shrank and split into parts, its fishing towns were left far from the water, and winds blew salty dust from the dry seabed onto nearby farms. Since 2005, a dam built with World Bank support has helped the northern part of the sea refill partly.

Area, which it stretches more and more toward the poles

items.q: People in Europe long called Southwest Asia and North Africa "the Middle East". What kind of direction does that name use?

Absolute direction: the region is east of the whole world
Absolute direction: it measures east from the North Pole
Relative distance: it measures how long the trip from Europe took

options: Space, the area between and around places on a map

items.q: Build an explanation of how time-space compression changes a pattern of distance decay.

specific.model: Because a new high-speed train cuts the trip from Lyon to Paris to about two hours, Paris feels closer, so more people from Lyon make day trips to Paris than before.

cause.label: Cause
options: a new high-speed train cuts the trip from Lyon to Paris to about two hours
Lyon and Paris are in France

why.1: That is true but changes nothing; the cause must be what made travel faster.

link.label: Link
options: Paris feels closer
Paris has moved closer in kilometers

why.1: The distance in kilometers does not change; the travel time does.

effect.label: Effect
options: more people from Lyon make day trips to Paris than before
fewer people travel at all

items.q: Which statement describes how people changed this hillside?

They cleared the whole hill of trees and built houses across the slope

Possibilism: the steep land set limits, but people chose a way to farm it

items.q: How could the stepped fields help make farming on this hillside sustainable?
options: The steps let farmers clear the forest at the top more quickly
The stone walls keep the river from flooding the two houses at the foot
The flat steps slow rainwater, so less soil washes down the slope
The steps make the hill taller, so it gets more sunlight

items.q: What can this drawing NOT tell you about the hillside?
options: Whether the slope has been changed by people
Whether there is a water channel
Whether crops are grown on the steps
Who built the steps, and when

items.q: Which change in land use started the sea's decline?

Fishing towns were built along the shore of the sea
Salty dust was blown onto nearby farms by the wind
A dam was built to hold water in the northern part

items.q: Why is the Aral Sea often used as an example of resource use that was not sustainable?
options: Cotton is a natural resource that will not grow again once it is picked
The rivers were used so heavily that the sea, its fish and nearby farms suffered
The sea was too far from big cities to be useful to the people of the region

items.q: The partial refilling of the northern sea after a dam was built shows which idea?

items.q: Place the two ideas about people and the environment in the order geographers held them, earlier to later.

slips.why: Possibilism came later, as a reaction against determinism: geographers showed people make choices in any environment.
Sustainability is a goal for using resources, not one of the two views of how the environment shapes people.

items.q: Around 1900, some writers claimed that hot climates made people less hardworking, so people from cooler lands should rule them. Which idea is this, and why was it rejected?
options: Possibilism; it gave people too much credit for adapting to their surroundings and climate
Sustainability; it said hot places should save their resources for the future
Environmental determinism; it was rejected because hot climates were too hard to study

items.q: Large parts of the Netherlands are land that people took from the sea and from lakes by building dikes and pumping out the water. Which idea does this support?

items.q: Las Vegas, Nevada, gets most of its water from the Colorado River, stored behind Hoover Dam in Lake Mead. Which statement about this is most accurate?
options: The desert climate made it impossible for a large city to grow in this place
A dam let the city grow in a dry climate, but it relies on a shared river

items.q: Which of these is a renewable natural resource?
options: Coal burned in a power plant
Oil pumped from under the ground
Sunlight used for electricity
Natural gas piped to homes

items.q: Off Newfoundland, Canada, heavy fishing caused the cod stock to collapse, and Canada banned commercial cod fishing in 1992. What does this show about sustainability?
options: Fish are a nonrenewable resource, like oil

items.q: In Manaus, Brazil, a stretch of rainforest is cleared for a new road and housing. Which concept describes this change?
options: A change in land use

items.q: Build an explanation of possibilism using a real place.

specific.frame: In ___, ___ limited people, but they ___, so ___.
specific.model: In the Netherlands, a low, flooded coast limited people, but they built dikes and pumped out the sea, so they could live and farm on land that had been under water.

place.label: Place
options: the Netherlands
a country somewhere

why.1: Too vague: name a real place.

limit.label: Environmental limit
options: a low, flooded coast
a large population

why.1: A large population is not a limit set by the physical environment.

choice.label: Human choice
options: built dikes and pumped out the sea
had to leave

items.q: The map covers the region of South Asia. At what scale of analysis are its data?

options: Each province has about half of its households above the middle income, like the nation
Country A earns more than its neighbors, as the national figure shows
Incomes are rising fastest in the Western Uplands and the Southern Forest
They cluster in the Capital Region and South Coast; few are in the Western Uplands

items.q: The national figure was made by adding up the households of all eight provinces into one number. What is this called, and what is its drawback?
options: Aggregated data; one value for all provinces hides how they differ
Qualitative data; it is built from words, so it is hard to put on a map
Remote sensing; it was measured by satellite, so it misses people
A spatial pattern; it shows where households are clustered

items.q: A large new port opens on the South Coast, linking it to world shipping. Which effect across scales is most likely?
options: The port changes nothing in Country A, because world trade happens at the global scale
Global trade brings jobs to the coast, so its gap with the uplands may widen
Incomes in each province rise by the same amount, because the port belongs to the nation
The Western Uplands gain the most, because they are farthest from the new port

items.q: At what scale of analysis should a minister read this map to decide which provinces get new job programs?
options: National, because the minister works for the whole country
Global, because jobs depend on world trade
Local (subnational), since the choice is between provinces
Regional, because Country A is part of a world region

items.q: Stack the four scales of analysis from the largest area at the top to the smallest at the bottom.

model.title: Scales of analysis, largest to smallest

slips.why: A region such as South Asia holds several countries, so it is larger than one nation.
Map scale is a ratio for drawing a map, not a scale of analysis.

items.q: A map of a United States presidential election colored by state shows large blocks of one color. A map of the same election by county shows cities voting differently from nearby rural counties. What does this show?
options: State maps are wrong and should not be used to report the results of an election
County maps show a different election from the one shown on the state map
Rural counties and cities vote the same way, as the state map shows
Patterns change with scale: county data show a city and rural divide that states hide

items.q: Rising world demand for avocados led farmers in Michoacán, Mexico, to plant more avocado orchards on hillsides that were forest. Which scales does this example link?
options: A global process (world demand) and a local change (land use in Michoacán)
A national process (Mexican law) and a global change (world climate)
A local process (one farm) and a regional change (across Latin America)
A regional process (South Asian trade) and a national change (Mexico's border)

items.q: A student finds that Brazil's national average rainfall is moderate and concludes that the city of Manaus gets moderate rain. Why is this conclusion weak?
options: Rainfall data are qualitative, so averaging them gives a misleading number
A national average is aggregated, so it hides very wet places like the Amazon
Manaus is outside Brazil, so Brazil's national data leave the city out
Rainfall is measured at the global scale, so national averages are wrong

items.q: Sea level is rising around the world as the oceans warm and land ice melts. Officials in Miami Beach, Florida, raise streets and install pumps. How do these scales relate?
options: A local process causes a global effect, which the national government answers
A national process causes a regional effect, which the world answers
A global process has a local effect, which a local government answers
The scales are unrelated, since Miami Beach's streets are local

items.q: Why might a national government and a city mayor reach different conclusions from the same health data?
options: One of the two is reading the data wrongly, since data give one answer
Health data are global, so neither leader can use them for a decision
Mayors use qualitative data, while national governments use quantitative data
Each reads the data at a different scale, with its own pattern

items.q: A world map shades each country by its share of people living in cities. A map of Japan shades each prefecture (a province of Japan) by people per square kilometer. At what scale of analysis are the data on each map?
options: World map: national, one value per country; Japan map: local, one value per prefecture
World map: global, as it covers the world; Japan map: national, as it covers one country
Both maps are at the local scale, because both measure where people live in cities
Both maps are at the global scale, because Japan also appears on the world map

items.q: Build a sentence that compares a pattern at two scales.

specific.frame: At the ___ scale, ___, whereas at the ___ scale, ___.
specific.model: At the national scale, Country A has half its households above the middle income, whereas at the local scale, the Capital Region is at 65% or more and the Western Uplands below 35%.

scaleA.label: First scale
options: national
global

why.1: The figure for all of Country A is national, not global.

patternA.label: Pattern at the first scale
options: Country A has half its households above the middle income
the map has eight provinces

why.1: That is a fact about the map, not a pattern in the data.

scaleB.label: Second scale
options: local
regional

why.1: Provinces inside one country are local, not regional.

patternB.label: Pattern at the second scale
options: the Capital Region is at 65% or more and the Western Uplands below 35%
incomes vary

why.1: Too vague: name the places and values.

items.q: What kind of region does this survey map?
options: A perceptual region, defined by what people believe
A formal region: it is defined by one trait that is measured
A functional region: it is organized around a center
A transition zone: it is defined by a change in climate

items.q: Describe the edge of "the North" shown on this map.
options: Sharp: each province is either fully in the region or fully out of it, with no middle
Fuzzy: in the Central Valley and Western Uplands, residents are split
It follows the South Coast, where most people say that they belong to the North
It is a straight line that a government drew across the country

items.q: Which province is most clearly at the heart of "the North"?
options: The Central Valley
The South Coast
The Northern Hills
The Capital Region

items.q: What is a limitation of this survey as a map of "the North"?
options: It is quantitative, so it says nothing about what people believe
It uses a choropleth, which is the wrong kind of map for showing percents
It shows an invented country, so the region it maps is not a real one to study
One value per province hides towns whose views differ from their province

items.q: The commuters tie these provinces to the capital. What kind of region do they define?
options: A functional region, organized around the capital
A formal region, where everyone shares one language
A perceptual region, drawn from what residents believe
A transition zone between two climates

items.q: Describe the pattern of commuting on this map.
options: The most commuters come from the Western Uplands, one of the provinces farthest away
Most come from the Central Valley, next to the capital; fewest from the far north and west
About the same number of commuters come from each of the seven provinces shown
The fewest commuters come from the provinces next to the capital

items.q: A fast train line opens from the Western Uplands to the capital. How would this region most likely change?
options: It would shrink, because faster trains push the capital away
It would turn into a formal region, because a train is one trait
It would reach farther west as more Western Uplands residents commute
It would stay the same, because regions keep the shape they were given

items.q: In Quebec, Canada, a large majority of people speak French as their first language. Which kind of region is Quebec in this sense?
options: A functional region
A perceptual region
A transition zone
A formal region

items.q: Which is the best example of a functional region?
options: The area a Denver newspaper delivers to each morning
The area where most people speak Spanish in the United States
The area Americans call "the Midwest"
The area where corn is the main crop in the United States

items.q: Ask Americans which states are in "the South" and you get different answers. Why?
options: It is a formal region with a border set in federal law, which people forget
It is a perceptual region, so its edges depend on what each person believes
It is a functional region tied to one city, Atlanta, by daily commuting
It is not a region, since it has no clear edges that everyone can agree on

items.q: Compare a formal region and a functional region.
options: Both are defined by what people believe about a place
A formal region is tied to a center, whereas a functional region shares a trait
Formal regions share a trait, whereas functional regions are tied to a center
Both have sharp edges that stay fixed as transport and trade change over time

items.q: The Sahel is a belt across Africa south of the Sahara, where desert slowly gives way to grassland. What kind of area is the Sahel?
options: A functional region organized around one city
A perceptual region drawn by surveys
A sharp line between the desert and the grassland
A transition zone between two formal regions

items.q: Some definitions of "the Middle East" include Egypt and Türkiye; others leave out one or both. What does this show about regions?
options: People draw regions for a purpose, so their edges can differ and be contested
The Middle East has no countries, so it is not a real region
There is one official map of the region, and the others are mistakes
Regions are set by the United Nations, and its map settles the argument

items.q: Which of these are regions at the local scale? Select all that apply.
options: The delivery area of a pizza shop in Toronto
A neighborhood in Lagos known for its markets
Southeast Asia
The European Union

items.q: Build a sentence that identifies a region, its type and the trait or tie that defines it.

specific.model: The area served by Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport is a functional region, because travelers from many nearby towns fly in and out through that one center.

region.label: Region
options: The area served by Atlanta's Hartsfield-Jackson airport
Some area

why.1: Too vague: name a real region.

type.label: Type
options: functional
formal
perceptual

why.1: A formal region shares a trait; the airport's area is tied by trips to a center.
why.2: A perceptual region rests on beliefs; this area is defined by travel to the airport.

tie.label: What defines it
options: travelers from many nearby towns fly in and out through that one center
it has a large airport

why.1: Having an airport is a feature; the region is defined by the trips people make to it.
